explanations: terra: The covenant joins good treatment of parents and kin with ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ and the needy, placing the orphan inside the community's closest obligations.

luna: The section's dictionary account of آل describes a household as a place of mutual return, while its central scene gives a child refuge at home. This ayah calls the Sacred House “مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ وَأَمْنًا,” a place people return to and find safety; it extends the home image to a shared sanctuary. | terra: God makes the House a place to which people return and a place of security, a public sacred counterpart to the section's home defined by mutual return and refuge.

luna: The section develops a home as both refuge and a place where dependents receive provision. In the verse after 2:125's Sacred House as a place of return and security, Abraham asks for the city to be safe and for its people to receive fruits; this ayah adds sustenance to the sanctuary's protection.

luna: The section develops giving what a household member needs and receiving a vulnerable child into family life. This ayah names giving wealth, despite love of it, to relatives and orphans; it makes generous provision for the orphan a mark of righteousness. | terra: Righteousness includes giving cherished wealth to kin, ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ, the needy, and travelers; the home opened to the orphan becomes a test of substantive piety.
terra: Spouses are “clothing” for one another, a reciprocal image of covering and closeness that makes concrete the source dictionary's marriage-as-fortress sense.

luna: When asked what to spend, this ayah names parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers as recipients. It connects the section's family-provider image to the concrete distribution of means to dependent people. | terra: The answer about spending names parents, relatives, ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ, the needy, and travelers, specifying where the recipient of provision must redirect what is given.

luna: The section describes a child being received into a household. In answering about orphans, this ayah permits living with them and calls them “فَإِخْوَانُكُمْ” (your brothers), framing care as shared family life rather than distance. | terra: The ruling on ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ says that setting their affairs right is best and that sharing life with them makes them “your brothers,” directly opening the household to the orphan.

luna: The section defines upbringing as taking a child from one stage to the next. This ayah sets a complete two-year nursing period and assigns the father provision and clothing, spelling out the household labor and material support that sustain early growth. | terra: Mothers nurse to completion while the father must provide food and clothing according to fairness, and neither parent is harmed through the child; this spells out the household's shared work of raising.
terra: Spending is not to be followed by reminders of generosity or injury, a precise ethical boundary between sheltering care and Pharaoh's weaponized recollection of nurture.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for قَهَرَ is to abase or humiliate the orphan. This ayah says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, setting a clear boundary: provision for a vulnerable person must not become a means of harming or degrading them. | terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, showing that provision which humiliates the recipient contradicts the house's softened heart.
terra: Believers must not nullify charity through reminders and harm; this gives the explicit rule violated when Pharaoh presents childhood care as leverage.
terra: In the spending passage, Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty; fear of becoming poor is exposed as a force that can close the providing hand.
terra: When a debtor is weak or unable to dictate, the guardian must dictate justly, giving the section's dependent weak person a concrete supporter and voice.
terra: Mary's mother entrusts the child still in her womb wholly to her Lord, beginning the passage in which a child is received, raised, and assigned a guardian.
terra: At Mary's birth her mother names her and commends her and her descendants to God's protection, supplying the parental act of entrustment that precedes the foster care of 3:37.

luna: The section describes a person who takes responsibility for a child and the provision available within a home. This ayah says “وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا” and that Zakariya found provision with Mary, showing a guardian's care joined to material sustenance. | terra: Mary's Lord gives her good growth, entrusts her to Zechariah, and he finds provision beside her; this directly joins the section's stage-by-stage raising, foster guardian, finding, and provision.

terra: Immediately after witnessing provision in his foster child's chamber, Zechariah asks his Lord for good offspring, making care of another's child and hope for one's own meet in a single household passage.
terra: The angels answer Zechariah with news of John while he stands praying, showing the guardian's own household enlarged by a divinely granted child.

luna: The section names the one who attends to a child as a caretaker. This ayah recounts the people casting lots over who would assume Mary's care (“أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ”), a direct scene of assigning guardianship. | terra: The casting of pens decides which man will sponsor Mary, showing that a child without her father requires a particular guardian rather than an abstract kindness.
terra: One soul, its mate, and the many men and women spread from the pair give a Quranic account of the household expanding through marriage and kinship.

luna: The section's guardian is responsible for a child in the home. This ayah orders guardians to give orphans their property and forbids consuming it into their own, spelling out a material duty that protects the dependent from the household's power. | terra: The orphan's property must be handed over intact rather than absorbed into the guardian's wealth, setting a concrete boundary on the power of the receiving household.

luna: The section says marriage enlarges a household. This ayah makes marriage with orphan girls conditional on fearing injustice to them, and directs men who fear that injustice to marry other women; it draws a boundary around taking an orphan into a marital household. | terra: Fear of injustice toward orphan girls governs whom and how many one may marry; the verse makes marriage inside an orphan-managing household answerable to justice.

luna: The section says a household includes those whose support one carries. This ayah calls wealth a means of support and directs people to provide food and clothing to those under their care, a specific parallel to the household provider's responsibility. | terra: Within the orphan-property passage, those not ready to manage wealth are still to be fed, clothed, and addressed kindly from it; guardianship joins preservation with daily care.

luna: The section defines the orphan as a child whose father died before maturity. This ayah tests orphans until they reach marriageable age and sound judgment, then orders their property returned; its endpoint closely matches the section's age boundary. | terra: Guardians test the orphans until marriageable age and sound judgment, then return their property; the verse also distinguishes a rich guardian from a poor one who may take fairly, exactly joining maturation with the poor provider.

luna: When relatives, orphans, and the needy are present at an inheritance division, this ayah says to give them provision from it and speak kindly. It puts the dependent and orphan inside the family distribution scene developed by the section. | terra: When orphans and needy people attend an estate division, they are to receive something and be addressed kindly, joining material care to non-humiliating speech.
terra: Guardians are told to imagine leaving weak offspring behind, fear for them, and speak rightly; the command makes another's vulnerable child feel like one's own.

luna: The section's home is meant to sustain a child. This ayah says those who consume orphan property unjustly consume fire into their bellies, a direct reversal of the provider's duty to protect and maintain the orphan. | terra: Those who consume orphan wealth unjustly consume fire into themselves; this is the receiving household transformed from guardian into predator.

luna: The section begins with a child whose father has died and discusses the support carried within a household. This ayah assigns inheritance shares to sons and daughters when a parent dies, giving the fatherless child's material situation a concrete legal counterpart, though it addresses inheritance rather than foster care.

luna: The section names الرَّابّ under root ر ب ب as the person who takes charge of a stepchild, and الرَّبِيبَة as the woman who nurtures a child. The verse uses “وَرَبَائِبُكُمُ اللَّاتِي فِي حُجُورِكُمْ” for stepdaughters in a man's care, making the household's fostering relation explicit. | terra: The verse names foster mothers and sisters through nursing and رَبَائِبُكُمُ ٱلَّٰتِى فِى حُجُورِكُمْ; it supplies the Quranic family-law boundary for the source dictionary's child raised in another's lap.
terra: The marriage ruling repeatedly uses the language of chastity and being guarded, giving lexical substance to the source dictionary's statement that marriage is a fortress for the unmarried.

terra: A believer without means to marry a free woman may marry a believing bondwoman through her people and with a proper dower; the verse treats marriage as guarded belonging available amid poverty.

luna: The section describes the household as including people whose livelihood is borne by another. This ayah ties a husband's household responsibility to his spending (“وَبِمَا أَنفَقُوا مِنْ أَمْوَالِهِم”), showing material provision as part of domestic care. | terra: The verse grounds responsibility for household maintenance in expenditure from one's wealth, a specific Quranic counterpart to the source dictionary's person who supports dependents.
terra: The command to worship God is immediately embodied in goodness to parents, kin, ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ, the needy, neighbors, companions, and travelers.

luna: This ayah names oppressed men, women, and children calling for rescue from a town of wrongdoers. It is a specific counter-scene to the section's vulnerable orphan and its command not to subdue him: children under power need someone to stand for them. | terra: Oppressed men, women, and children ask God for a protecting ally and helper, turning the section's vulnerable child and supporting household into a communal rescue imperative.
terra: The truly weakened men, women, and children cannot devise a plan or يَهْتَدُونَ سَبِيلًا, a close Quranic counterpart to the source dictionary's weak person unable to proceed without support.

luna: The section makes home a place of shelter. This ayah describes leaving one's home in migration and finding on earth “مُرَاغَمًا كَثِيرًا وَسَعَةً” (room and spaciousness), a specific promise that displacement can open into refuge.

luna: The section develops a household enlarged by marriage and the care of children. This ayah specifically names orphan women whose prescribed rights are withheld while men desire to marry them; it exposes the household's power to exploit the person it should shelter and makes justice a condition of marriage. | terra: The ruling names orphan women whose prescribed rights are withheld in the very context of desired marriage, and commands justice for orphans.
terra: If spouses separate, God can enrich each from His abundance; the ayah bounds the source dictionary's marriage–غِنَى link by showing divine enrichment also beyond marriage.

luna: The section quotes root ق ه ر in تَقْهَرْ as humiliating or subduing an orphan. This ayah calls God “الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ,” the subduer over His servants; the contrast distinguishes divine sovereignty from a person's abuse of someone dependent. | terra: God alone is ٱلْقَاهِرُ over His servants; this different Quranic use of the source's qahr root marks the boundary between divine sovereignty and the human domination forbidden toward an orphan.

terra: The repeated statement that God is the Subduer over His servants reinforces that ultimate qahr belongs to God, while the receiving house is commanded to renounce humiliating power over the child.

luna: The section describes a household whose members return to one another and a child taken in from aloneness. This ayah says people will come to God “فُرَادَىٰ” and have left behind what they were given; it contrasts family support with each person's final solitude, though فردًا here means individually rather than the section's narrower sense of a rare, unmatched single thing.
terra: Children must not be killed from poverty, for God provides for parent and child; it reverses the section's poor provider into the false claim that poverty cancels care.

luna: The section places the orphan's vulnerability before his reaching maturity. This ayah forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best manner until he reaches maturity, making the guardian's restraint last through the child's dependence. | terra: One may approach the orphan's property only in the best manner until maturity, defining care as preservation across the child's growth.
terra: The mate is created from the same soul so that one may find rest with her, and the pair then carry a child; the ayah shows a household beginning in shelter and growing.

luna: The section's dictionary form آوى under root ء و ي means taking another into one's home. This ayah recalls a small, weakened community and says God gave them refuge, support, and provision (“فَآوَاكُمْ وَأَيَّدَكُم بِنَصْرِهِ وَرَزَقَكُم”); it expands household shelter into communal protection. | terra: The community is recalled as few and made weak, after which God shelters them, strengthens them, and provides good things; it expands the orphan's sequence from vulnerability to shelter and provision.

luna: This ayah assigns a share of war gains to orphans, the needy, and travelers. The section's dependent household is one setting for provision; this verse extends provision to orphans through a public distribution. | terra: A fixed share of spoils is assigned to ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ and the needy, turning care of the fatherless into a public claim on communal wealth.

luna: The section's dictionary form آوى describes sheltering another. This ayah names believers who migrated and those who gave refuge and help (“آوَوا وَّنَصَرُوا”), presenting shelter as a reciprocal community duty. | terra: Those who gave refuge and aid to emigrants become their protecting allies; shelter creates a relation of mutual responsibility like the section's enlarged household.

luna: This ayah repeats the section's sheltering scene with believers who “آوَوا وَّنَصَرُوا,” then connects that support to forgiveness and provision. It shows the receiving household as part of a wider practice of refuge. | terra: The believers who migrated and those who sheltered and helped them are declared true believers, making reception of the vulnerable a defining bond.
terra: After the bonds created by migration, shelter, and aid, blood relatives are declared closer to one another in the legal order, marking a boundary between received communal kinship and lineage.
terra: Even a hostile outsider who asks protection must be granted refuge and then conveyed to safety; shelter here creates a temporary duty toward a vulnerable stranger.

luna: The section's dictionary form الغِنَى under root غ ن ي names marriage as one kind of enrichment. This ayah uses the same root in يُغْنِيكُم in a promise of material sufficiency after the fear of poverty (عَيْلَة); the financial sense marks a boundary from the section's marriage sense.
terra: Noah is told to carry his family into the ark except those already excluded, making the vessel a household refuge while marking that refuge's divinely set boundary.
terra: Noah calls his son to board with the family, but the son remains apart; a father's offered refuge can be refused.
terra: Noah's son says he will take refuge on a mountain, but no protector exists that day except divine mercy; physical shelter without the Lord reaches its limit.
terra: Noah appeals that his son is of his household, bringing the claim of family belonging before God after the failed rescue.
terra: God says the son is not of Noah's household because his conduct is unrighteous, setting a severe boundary on biological belonging as shelter.
terra: Unable to protect his guests, Lot wishes for strength or a powerful refuge; the scene exposes what a householder needs in order to shelter those who enter his home.
terra: A caravan finds a hidden boy and greets him as merchandise rather than making him family, a dark counter-scene to finding the vulnerable child and sheltering him.
terra: Joseph is sold for a paltry price after being found, showing the child commodified before the receiving household of 12:21 gives him an honored lodging.
terra: The Egyptian tells his wife to honor Joseph's lodging and considers taking him as a son, a direct scene of a displaced boy being received into a home.
terra: After Joseph is received into the Egyptian home in 12:21, this ayah brings him to full maturity and gives him judgment and knowledge, completing the fostered child's growth.
terra: In the house that received him, Joseph says his rabb has made his lodging good; whether rabb here is read as God or master, the wording activates the source's meeting of Lord and householder.
terra: Joseph asks whether many lords are better than God, the One, the Subduer; house-masters and ٱلْقَهَّارُ meet here to reserve ultimate qahr for God, unlike human humiliation of an orphan.
terra: A father entrusting another son says that God is the best guardian and most merciful, closely matching the section's claim that the vulnerable child ultimately has a Lord beyond human carers.
terra: The father seeks a solemn pledge that his son will be brought back unless the brothers are overpowered, showing a human guardian trying to secure the child's return while admitting his limits.

luna: The section's dictionary form آوى means taking someone into one's shelter. When Joseph's brothers arrive, he takes his brother Benjamin close to himself (“آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ”), making shelter an intimate act within a separated family. | terra: Joseph ءَاوَىٰٓ إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ, drawing his brother into his own protected space and beginning the family's return to him.
terra: Joseph answers the brothers who expelled him with no reproach and a prayer for mercy, supplying the softened heart that permits the family's later return into his care.

luna: The section's dictionary account of آل describes a household whose members return to one another. Joseph sends his shirt to his father and tells his brothers to bring the family; this ayah begins the reunion that arrives in 12:99 and is completed in 12:100. | terra: Joseph commands his brothers to bring their whole family to him, initiating the household reunion completed when he shelters his parents in 12:99.

luna: The section describes separated kin returning to one another. This ayah has Jacob recognize Joseph's scent as the caravan departs, a specific moment of a father's recognition before reunion; the link is limited because this verse does not itself show a household receiving anyone.

luna: The section's household is a place people return to and are received. Joseph takes his parents to himself (“آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ”) and welcomes them into Egypt; this portrays a grown child making a secure home for his family. | terra: Joseph ءَاوَىٰٓ إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ and welcomes the family into safety, reversing his own childhood reception into care for his parents.

luna: The section's dictionary account of آل describes a household whose return is to one another. After the family enters in 12:99, this ayah shows Joseph's parents and family reunited around him, completing the return of kin to a household. | terra: After 12:99's reception of his parents, Joseph raises them to the throne and names God's subtle care through the family's reunion, completing the formerly displaced child's reversal of role.

luna: The section describes a household with dependents and a person who provides for them. Abraham says he settled some of his descendants in a barren valley beside the Sacred House and asks God to provide fruits for its people, making the household's dependence on provision explicit.

luna: The section's child is sheltered after loss and vulnerability. This ayah promises those who migrated after being wronged that God will settle them in a good place, carrying the image of refuge into a new home after persecution.
terra: Spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision appear in one divine gift, closely matching the section's house enlarged through marriage and sustained by provision.

luna: The section defines عِيَال الرجل as the people whose support he carries. This ayah's parable depicts a person unable to act who is a burden on his master, a specific image of dependence and another's responsibility for a dependent; the context is a parable about worship, not a child or household.

luna: This ayah says God made houses for people as places of rest (“سَكَنًا”), giving a direct account of what the section's receiving home provides: settled shelter for those who live in it. | terra: God makes human houses places of rest, stating directly the sheltering function that the section's received child discovers in a home.

luna: The section describes household members returning care to one another, including the grown child who serves the family. This ayah commands gentle speech and humility toward aging parents; 17:24 then grounds that return in their raising the speaker when small. This verse's own contribution is the concrete conduct owed to the parents. | terra: When parents reach old age in one's care, the grown child must neither rebuke nor repel them but speak nobly; this is the section's reversal from being raised to sheltering one's former carers.

luna: The section's dictionary form رَبَّاهُ means “he raised him.” This ayah asks for mercy for parents “كَمَا رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا,” because they raised the speaker when small; it makes childhood care and its return in mercy explicit. | terra: The grown child asks for mercy on the parents كَمَا رَبَّيَانِى صَغِيرًا; the source's raising verb and softened heart become a precise reversal of care received in childhood.
terra: Children must not be killed for fear of poverty because God provides for them and their parents; imagined scarcity cannot close the household against its child.

luna: The section defines yatim as fatherless until maturity and then turns to how the orphan should be treated. This ayah protects the orphan's property “حَتَّىٰ يَبْلُغَ أَشُدَّهُ” and supplies the same endpoint for that protection. | terra: The orphan's property is protected until maturity, matching both the source definition's pre-puberty limit and the household's duty to bring the child safely to completion.

luna: The section's dictionary form آوى names taking refuge. This ayah says the young men sought refuge in the cave and asked for mercy and right direction, a scene of vulnerable youths turning to shelter when their surroundings fail them. | terra: The youths take refuge in the cave and ask their Lord for mercy and sound direction, linking physical shelter with the Lord's compassionate guidance.

luna: The young men in 18:10 seek refuge from their people; this ayah completes that scene with their companion's instruction to take refuge in the cave (“فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ”). Its own contribution is the practical act of finding a protected place. | terra: The youths are told to seek refuge in the cave, where their Lord will spread mercy and prepare ease in their affair; a non-house becomes the sheltering household of the image.

luna: The section defines رَبَّاهُ under root ر ب ب as raising a child through stages, and makes the orphan's reaching maturity the endpoint. This ayah names two orphan boys, protects their property, and says their Lord intended them to reach full strength (يَبْلُغَا أَشُدَّهُمَا); it makes the same care concrete as protection over time. | terra: The two boys are explicitly يَتِيمَيْنِ; their righteous father's treasure is preserved until they reach maturity, and رَبُّكَ wills that growth as mercy, gathering orphanhood, guardianship, maturation, and the Lord in one scene.
terra: Ishmael commands his household to prayer and almsgiving, portraying a family member actively tending the house's moral and material obligations.
terra: Moses asks for a helper “from my family,” locating needed support inside kinship rather than solitary strength.
terra: The requested brother is to strengthen Moses' back, a nonlexical Quranic counterpart to the source's weak person proceeding by leaning on others.

luna: The section defines upbringing as carrying a child through stages toward completion. In Moses' infancy, God says “وَلِتُصْنَعَ عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي” (that you be brought up under My care), placing the child’s protection and upbringing under a watchful guardian. | terra: The infant Moses is cast where an enemy household will take him, while God places love on him and has him formed “under My eye”; hostile surroundings become divine nurture.

luna: This retelling of Moses' rescue says his sister offers to identify someone who will care for him, then he is returned to his mother so she may be comforted and not grieve. It repeats the section's scene of a vulnerable child placed in care and protected through reunion. | terra: Moses' sister leads to someone who will care for him, and he is returned to his mother before God brings him through successive trials; separation, foster care, reunion, and formation all meet here.
terra: “Our Lord” gives each thing its created form and then guides it; giving, guidance, and stage-wise fitting meet in one account of divine nurture.

luna: The section describes a householder and the people whose needs he carries. This ayah commands the Prophet to enjoin prayer on his family and says God provides for him, connecting household responsibility to care that includes spiritual instruction as well as material support. | terra: The addressee must command his household to prayer and persevere, while God says “We provide for you”; household responsibility rests on divine provision rather than abundance in the provider.
terra: Human creation is narrated through successive bodily states until maturity, a direct Quranic analogue for the source dictionary's raising “state by state to completion.”
terra: One created state is transformed into another through embryo, bones, flesh, and a new creation, an extended concrete parallel to raising something state by state.

luna: The section's dictionary form آوى means to shelter someone. This ayah says God sheltered Mary and her son on a secure height with flowing water (“وَآوَيْنَاهُمَا إِلَىٰ رَبْوَةٍ ذَاتِ قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ”), pairing protection with a place to live and sustenance. | terra: Mary and her son are made a sign and given refuge on secure high ground with flowing water, an explicit mother-child shelter joined to provision.

luna: The section's dictionary form الغِنَى under root غ ن ي calls marriage a form of enrichment and a fortress for the unmarried. This ayah commands marriage for the unmarried and says that if they are poor God will enrich them (“إِن يَكُونُوا فُقَرَاءَ يُغْنِهِمُ اللَّهُ”), directly meeting that secondary sense. | terra: The command to marry the unmarried says that if they are poor God will enrich them, directly realizing the source dictionary's connection between غِنَى and marriage.

luna: The section's dictionary form الغِنَى under root غ ن ي includes marriage as a kind of enrichment. After 24:32 addresses marrying the unmarried, this ayah speaks of those who cannot find means to marry and tells them to remain chaste until God enriches them; it supplies the boundary case to the section's marriage-as-fortress image. | terra: Those unable to find means for marriage remain chaste until God enriches them; marriage and enrichment are again held together, now across a period of waiting.

terra: The source dictionary explicitly calls the rare solitary thing a “unique pearl”; the ayah's singular كَوْكَبٌ دُرِّىٌّ may therefore echo that secondary valuation, though it describes a radiant star rather than a child.
terra: Household servants and children below puberty must ask permission at three private times, giving the growing child a defined place and duty within the home.
terra: Once the household's children reach puberty they ask permission like adults, marking the same maturation boundary built into the source definition of orphanhood.
terra: The blind, lame, and sick are explicitly free to eat in a wide network of family houses, and people may eat together; weakness is included rather than shut outside the home.
terra: From created humanity God establishes both blood lineage and marriage ties, distinguishing the two relations through which the section's house grows.

luna: The section treats a home as a family whose members return to one another. This prayer asks for spouses and descendants who are “قُرَّةَ أَعْيُنٍ,” a household that brings comfort to the eyes, giving the family relation a specific emotional form. | terra: The prayer asks that spouses and offspring become comfort to the eyes, presenting the enlarged household as a gift requiring righteous formation.

luna: The section's dictionary branch under root ر ب ب says a man “raised his child”; Pharaoh uses the same raising sense in “أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا” (“Did we not raise you among us as a child?”). The question turns upbringing into a claim of debt; 26:22 supplies Moses' answer and exposes the coercive setting. | terra: Pharaoh's أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا matches the remembered-care question and the source dictionary's raising of a child, but makes the foster household itself the speaker.
terra: After citing Moses' upbringing in 26:18, Pharaoh calls him ungrateful; the ayah shows exactly how recalled care is converted into moral coercion.
terra: After recalling his flight in fear, Moses says his Lord gave him judgment and made him a messenger; divine formation answers Pharaoh's claim in 26:18 that Pharaoh's house made him.

luna: Moses calls the alleged favor “وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ تَمُنُّهَا عَلَيَّ” and identifies Israel's enslavement as its substance. This completes 26:18's reminder of being raised in Pharaoh's house, marking the boundary between care that protects a child and power that uses care as leverage. | terra: Moses exposes the supposed foster “favor” as inseparable from enslaving Israel; it is the section's direct counter-scene to divine care that becomes care for others rather than a debt.
terra: Pharaoh's policy slaughters sons and weakens their people; it supplies the violent household background against which his family receives Moses in 28:8-9.

luna: The section centers on a vulnerable child whose safety depends on another's care. This ayah shows Moses' mother nursing him and placing him in the river under God's instruction; 28:8 completes the sequence when Pharaoh's household picks him up. This ayah's own contribution is the mother's protective act during separation. | terra: God tells Moses' mother to nurse him, promises to return him, and answers her fear at the moment she must release him; divine guardianship holds the broken household together.

luna: The section presents being taken into a home as refuge. Here Pharaoh's household takes in Moses, yet the verse calls him a future enemy and grief to them; it is a specific reversal showing that a household can receive a child without becoming a merciful shelter. | terra: Pharaoh's household picks up the exposed infant, so the source dictionary's آل as a returning household meets the found child's entry into the very house that threatens his people.

luna: Pharaoh's wife asks that the infant be spared and says he may become “قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ لِي وَلَكَ” or be taken as a son. The section's home receives a vulnerable child; this scene makes the household's decision to welcome and protect a child explicit. | terra: Pharaoh's wife forbids killing the found infant and proposes taking him as a son, turning the persecutor's house, provisionally, into refuge.
terra: Moses' mother's heart becomes empty after separation and nearly reveals him until God steadies her, exposing the wound that the return in 28:13 heals.
terra: The mother sends Moses' sister to trace him from a distance, and the child's family quietly maintains connection before the foster-household offer in 28:12.

luna: The section's child is taken into a household and entrusted to a caretaker. Moses' sister offers “أَهْلِ بَيْتٍ يَكْفُلُونَهُ لَكُمْ” (a household to care for him), showing how a vulnerable child can be placed with a family while his mother is absent. | terra: Moses' sister offers an أَهْلِ بَيْتٍ who will undertake his care and sincerely look after him, an exact Quranic household for the section's received child.

luna: The section's sheltering of a fatherless child is joined here to safe reunion: God returns the infant to his mother so that she may be comforted and not grieve. This completes the care arrangement proposed in 28:12. | terra: God returns the separated infant to his mother so that her eye may be comforted and she not grieve; the sheltering household repairs a broken parent-child bond.
terra: After Moses' foster-household story, reaching full strength brings wisdom and knowledge; it is the completed-growth endpoint implicit in the source dictionary's tarbiya.
terra: As a displaced fugitive heading toward Midian, Moses asks his Lord to guide him on the right way; that guidance leads into the receiving household of 28:23-27.
terra: The two women hold back from the well because their father is old; this supplies the weak household whose need Moses answers in 28:24-27.
terra: Moses waters for the two women and then admits his own need for whatever good God sends; the needy outsider first serves a vulnerable household and then is received by it.
terra: One woman comes to Moses and leads him to her father, who tells him he is safe; guidance, a softened response, and entry into a protective home converge.
terra: The daughter asks her father to hire Moses as strong and trustworthy, turning the outsider's help into sustained service within the household formed in 28:27.

luna: The section says marriage enlarges the household and that a child may work for the family and bring what it asks. In this ayah, Moses' work for a household leads to a marriage proposal with its daughter; it is a specific meeting of domestic service and marriage, though not a literal bride being led to her husband. | terra: The father offers Moses marriage to a daughter in exchange for years of service, forming a household around a displaced poor man through marriage and work.
terra: Moses accepts the marriage-and-service arrangement without injustice between the two terms and makes God witness, completing the fair household compact begun in 28:27.
terra: God promises to strengthen Moses' arm through his brother, making family support the answer to confessed weakness.

luna: The section describes marriage as a way the household grows and invokes its dictionary gloss of marriage as a fortress for the unmarried. This ayah describes spouses as a source of tranquility, affection, and mercy, making the household's sheltering function explicit. | terra: Spouses are created so that one may dwell in tranquility with the other, with affection and mercy placed between them; this gives Quranic substance to marriage as a sheltering fortress.
terra: God creates from weakness, gives strength, and returns strength to weakness; the sequence illuminates why the household's supporting roles eventually reverse.

luna: The section describes gradual raising toward maturity. This ayah names a mother's carrying “وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ” and the child's weaning in two years, giving a bodily account of dependence and care as the child grows. | terra: The mother's weakness upon weakness and two years of weaning specify the labor by which a child is raised and ground the child's later gratitude.
terra: After 31:14 recalls parental nurture, this ayah refuses obedience when parents demand idolatry yet still commands kind worldly companionship, setting a boundary without dissolving care.
terra: No parent can avail a child nor a child a parent on the final day, setting the eschatological limit of the household's mutual support.

luna: The section describes a child whose father has died and a separate adult who takes responsibility for raising him. This ayah says “وَمَا جَعَلَ أَدْعِيَاءَكُمْ أَبْنَاءَكُمْ,” setting a boundary between caring for a child and claiming that he is one's biological son. | terra: God has not made adopted sons biological sons; the verse preserves a legal boundary even while the section dignifies raising another's child.

luna: This ayah says adopted children should be called by their fathers (“ادْعُوهُمْ لِآبَائِهِمْ”), completing 33:4's distinction. It clarifies that a household can care for a child while preserving his lineage. | terra: Adopted children are called by their fathers, and those whose fathers are unknown remain brothers in faith and protected associates; lost paternity does not erase belonging, but its form is defined.
terra: The Prophet's wives receive the relational title of believers' mothers while blood relatives retain priority in law, another precise boundary around nonbiological household belonging.
terra: The former wife of an adopted son is not treated by the law as a biological son's wife, a marriage boundary around the foster relation developed in the section.
terra: Human beings are the poor in relation to God while God is ٱلْغَنِىُّ; this theological dependence clarifies why even the householder who provides remains one sustained by the Lord.
terra: Human beings are created in their mothers' wombs “creation after creation,” a particularly close Quranic formulation of the source dictionary's stage-by-stage nurture toward completion.
terra: The human being is brought from created stages to infancy, full strength, and old age, extending the section's child-growth image across an entire life.
terra: God grants daughters or sons as He wills, placing the house's growth under divine giving rather than human possession.
terra: Paired sons and daughters or childlessness complete 42:49's account, marking the limits around how a household grows.

luna: This ayah describes pregnancy, birth, and weaning before a person reaches maturity. It parallels the section's growth from dependence toward adulthood, while making the parent's labor behind that growth perceptible. | terra: Pregnancy, birth, nursing, maturity, and the adult's prayer for parents and offspring trace care across stages and generations, closely matching growth toward completion.
terra: People are invited to spend yet some withhold, while God is rich and they are poor; the poor householder's dependence therefore does not cancel the call to give.

luna: The section describes those who carry the living of others and the needy who can themselves support a household. This ayah says a recognized share of the righteous people's wealth belongs to the asker and the deprived, making the provider's responsibility toward the needy explicit.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of yatim includes a unique, rare pearl. This ayah compares the young attendants of Paradise to “لُؤْلُؤٌ مَّكْنُونٌ” (protected pearls), a specific but indirect echo of the section's pearl image; it does not describe an orphan. | terra: Young attendants circulate among the household “like hidden pearls”; the verse uniquely meets both source dictionary details of the serving boy and the child figured as a precious pearl.
terra: The ayah states that God is the one who enriches and grants sufficiency, a repeated direct formulation of the Lord's act in finding the poor person and enriching him.
terra: Everlasting youths circulate in service, corresponding to the source dictionary's child working within the household.
terra: The cups, pitchers, and drink carried by the youths of 56:17 specify the things they place into others' hands, completing that secondary dictionary scene.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of yatim includes the image of a unique pearl. This ayah likens its companions to “اللُّؤْلُؤِ الْمَكْنُونِ” (protected pearls), a limited parallel in value and preciousness, without depicting a fatherless child. | terra: The comparison to hidden pearls may echo the source dictionary's explicit “unique pearl” valuation, though this ayah applies the pearl image to heavenly companions rather than to a solitary child.

luna: This ayah directs that shared gains reach relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so wealth does not circulate only among the rich. It extends the section's household support for dependents into a community measure. | terra: Fay is directed to ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ and the needy so that wealth does not merely circulate among the rich, making household care part of a wider distributive order.
terra: This ayah identifies those welcomed in 59:9 as poor emigrants expelled from their homes and property, supplying the homelessness and need to which the host household responds.

luna: The section describes a household that receives and provides for someone in need. This ayah praises the people who settled in the home before the emigrants, loved those who came to them, and preferred them over themselves even when needy; it is a direct host-and-refuge community. | terra: The people settled in the home love those who migrate to them and prefer them despite their own privation; it is a communal version of the poor household that shelters and provides.
terra: Some spouses and children can become enemies, yet believers are told to pardon and forgive; the ayah both limits idealized household safety and preserves the softened response.
terra: Wealth and children are a trial rather than possessions that guarantee honor, placing a boundary around the expanding, provisioned household of the section.
terra: The verse commands lodging women where one lives, support through pregnancy, payment for nursing, and fair consultation, making shelter and infant care concrete household duties.

terra: A person of restricted provision must still spend from what God has given, and God promises ease after hardship; this directly illuminates the section's poor person who nevertheless maintains dependents.

luna: The section presents the home as a place where someone takes responsibility for others. This ayah directly commands believers to protect themselves and their families from the Fire, extending the household's caretaker role to their family's ultimate well-being. | terra: Believers must guard both themselves and their families from the Fire, stating the householder's protective responsibility at its widest boundary.
terra: The wives of Noah and Lot live under righteous husbands yet the household bond cannot protect them from God, another boundary on family as ultimate refuge.
terra: Pharaoh's wife asks God for a house near Him and rescue from Pharaoh, replacing an oppressive earthly household with divine refuge.
terra: The sinner would ransom himself with his sons, reversing the householder's duty to protect children into sacrificing them for himself.
terra: Spouse and brother are added to the family members the sinner would surrender, undoing the mutual return that defines the source's household.
terra: He would even ransom the clan ٱلَّتِى تُـْٔوِيهِ, the very family that used to shelter him; received refuge is betrayed rather than repaid through care.

luna: The section describes dependents whose support someone bears. This ayah says the righteous have a known right in their wealth; 70:25 identifies the asker and the deprived as those who receive it. This verse's own contribution is that support is an established claim on wealth.

luna: The section links household provision to those in need. This ayah identifies the recipients of the known right named in 70:24 as the asker and the deprived, specifying whose need the wealth is meant to answer.
terra: God has created people in stages, succinctly stating the staged formation that the source dictionary places inside the meaning of raising.
terra: The addressee is told not to confer favor seeking increase, reinforcing the section's distinction between a divine gift that opens the hand and a favor used as a claim.

luna: The section's home takes in a needy child; this ayah describes feeding an orphan, a needy person, and a captive out of love for God. It makes provision for the vulnerable a chosen act rather than a claim on them. | terra: The righteous feed the needy, the orphan, and the captive despite their own desire for the food, enacting provision from a household that may itself have little.
terra: Linked to 76:8's feeding of the orphan, the carers seek neither repayment nor thanks; their care directly reverses Pharaoh's use of upbringing as a claim against Moses.
terra: Vessels and cups are circulated among the blessed; read with the youths identified in 76:19, this supplies the objects handed in the section's secondary child-service scene.
terra: The silver-crystal vessels are measured exactly, adding the prepared household service whose attendants appear in 76:19.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of yatim includes a rare pearl. This ayah compares the young attendants to “لُؤْلُؤًا مَّنثُورًا” (scattered pearls); it supplies a concrete pearl image, though its context is not orphanhood. | terra: Everlasting youths circulate in service and appear like scattered pearls, again joining the section's child who hands the household what it wants with its “orphan pearl” valuation.
terra: The act of frowning and turning away is a close behavioral reverse of receiving a vulnerable person with the softened heart developed in the section.
terra: This ayah identifies the person slighted in 80:1 as blind, making the reversal concern an actual dependent seeker rather than discourtesy in the abstract.
terra: The correction asks whether the blind visitor might purify himself, identifying moral possibility in the vulnerable person whom 80:1-2 slighted.
terra: The blind visitor may receive a reminder that benefits him, completing why turning away from him mistakes his worth.
terra: On that day a person flees from his brother, reversing the household whose members ordinarily return to and support one another.
terra: Flight extends to mother and father, setting an eschatological limit on the parent-child care that the section traces across generations.
terra: Spouse and children complete the household from which each person flees, the full reverse of marriage enlarging a sheltering home.
terra: The buried girl is summoned as a speaking party on Judgment Day, restoring standing to the child whom a household cast out of life.
terra: Her question asks for what sin she was killed, exposing the furthest possible opposite of receiving and raising a vulnerable child.
terra: The human being reads the Lord's generous provision as personal honor; 89:17 then tests that claim by whether the orphan is honored, linking received bounty to household conduct.
terra: Restricted provision is misread as the Lord's humiliation, but 89:17 immediately redirects attention to humans who fail to honor the orphan; poverty itself is not the disgrace.

luna: The section turns from being sheltered to the command not to humiliate an orphan. This ayah rebukes people who do not honor the orphan, a direct social reversal of the home that receives the child. | terra: لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ ٱلْيَتِيمَ names the house that withholds honor, the explicit reverse of sheltering the child and refusing to humiliate him.

luna: The section moves from receiving an orphan to its opposite, neglecting the vulnerable. This ayah condemns failure to encourage feeding the needy; beside 89:17's failure to honor the orphan, it shows that both dignity and material care are denied. | terra: Following 89:17's failure to honor the orphan, people also fail to urge feeding the needy; the closed door affects both the fatherless child and the poor.

luna: The section says the orphan must not be humiliated and describes the household as responsible for dependents. This ayah condemns devouring inheritance greedily; beside 89:17, it may evoke exploitation of an orphan's inheritance, though the verse itself does not specify whose inheritance. | terra: Immediately after failing to honor the orphan and feed the poor, people consume inheritance greedily; the ayah shows how the closed household can turn a vulnerable person's estate into prey.
terra: This ayah supplies the act governing 90:15: feeding on a day of hunger, so care for the kin-orphan is costly provision rather than a sentiment.

luna: The section identifies the orphan by the loss of a father. This ayah names an orphan who is close of kin and must be fed in a day of hunger, joining kinship, need, and concrete support. | terra: The difficult ascent includes feeding يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ, an orphan who is also kin, so the vulnerable child is explicitly within the family circle.

luna: The section connects an orphan's vulnerability with those who support people in need. After 90:15 names the orphan near of kin, this ayah adds feeding “مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ,” the person in extreme want; it completes the passage's scene of feeding the vulnerable. | terra: Alongside the kin-orphan of 90:15 stands a destitute person in misery, echoing the section's movement from orphanhood to poverty within one field of care.
terra: After the feeding of the orphan and destitute in 90:14-16, believers counsel one another to mercy, naming the softened heart that sustains the section's household.
terra: The Godfearing person gives wealth to purify himself, supplying the active generosity toward which the recipient of divine care is turned.
terra: Linked to 92:18's giving, no one's favor is being repaid; this is the clean opposite of Pharaoh converting foster care into an outstanding debt.
terra: Linked to 92:18-19, the giver seeks only the face of the Most High Lord, locating care's motive outside household status or repayment.
terra: The giver “will surely be satisfied,” echoing 93:5's promise of satisfaction while showing the satisfaction alongside generous care rather than possession.

terra: The same addressee is met with another intimate “Have We not?” reminder of divine care, this time the opening of his breast; it reinforces the stance of 93:6 without replacing its orphan scene.
terra: The human being transgresses, with 96:7 identifying the trigger as imagined self-sufficiency; enrichment that forgets dependence produces the opposite of the section's commanded care.
terra: أَن رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ makes self-perceived independence the cause of tyranny, a pointed reversal of being enriched by the Lord and then protecting the vulnerable.

luna: The section's dictionary form رَبُّ الدَّارِ means the owner of a house. This ayah calls God “رَبَّ هَٰذَا الْبَيْتِ,” the Lord of this House, directly joining the house image to its sustaining master. | terra: رَبَّ هَٰذَا ٱلْبَيْتِ names the Lord of the House, giving a Quranic meeting for the source dictionary's “owner of the house” while retaining the divine Lord.

luna: The section joins shelter to the household's material needs. This ayah says the Lord of the House fed its people against hunger and secured them from fear (“أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ وَآمَنَهُم مِّنْ خَوْفٍ”), completing the house's role as provider and refuge begun in 106:3. | terra: Linked to 106:3's Lord of the House, this ayah says He feeds against hunger and secures against fear, the two basic acts of the sheltering, provisioning home.

terra: The question “Have you seen the one who denies the Judgment?” is answered by 107:2's treatment of the orphan, paralleling the section's use of a question to expose what remembered care must produce.

luna: The section ends by forbidding the humiliation of an orphan. This ayah depicts the contrary act, one who “يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ” (shoves the orphan away), making the denied shelter visible as rejection. | terra: The denier يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ, violently pushing away the very child whom the section's house takes in.

luna: The section places an orphan's dignity beside the provider's responsibility. This ayah condemns failure to urge feeding the needy; beside 107:2's shoving of the orphan, it shows rejection joined to withholding care. | terra: Beside 107:2's repulsion of the orphan, failure to urge feeding the poor joins the two vulnerable figures that 93:6-9 places in one moral sequence.
